claim: There is no spatio-temporally resolved method to measure the release of neuropeptides in vivo.
source: Research on neuropeptide function has advanced rapidly, yet there is still no spatio-temporally resolved method to measure the release of neuropeptides in vivo.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a gap in current research capabilities.

claim: Neuropeptide Release Reporters (NPRRs) are novel genetically-encoded sensors with high temporal resolution and genetic specificity.
source: Here we introduce Neuropeptide Release Reporters (NPRRs): novel genetically-encoded sensors with high temporal resolution and genetic specificity.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, stated in the abstract.

claim: NPRRs recapitulate the trafficking and packaging of native neuropeptides.
source: Using the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) as a model, we provide evidence that NPRRs recapitulate the trafficking and packaging of native neuropeptides
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NPRRs report stimulation-evoked neuropeptide release events as real-time changes in fluorescence intensity with sub-second temporal resolution.
source: and report stimulation-evoked neuropeptide release events as real-time changes in fluorescence intensity, with sub-second temporal resolution.
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging experiments showing fluorescence changes in response to electrical stimulation.

claim: Neuropeptides exert an important but complex influence on neural function and behavior.
source: Neuropeptides (NPs) exert an important but complex influence on neural function and behavior (Hökfelt et al., 2000; Insel and Young, 2000; Nässel and Winther, 2010; Bargmann and Marder, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: A major lacuna in the study of neuropeptides is the lack of a method for imaging NP release in vivo with subcellular spatial resolution and subsecond temporal resolution.
source: A major lacuna in the study of NPs is the lack of a method for imaging NP release in vivo, with subcellular spatial resolution and subsecond temporal resolution.
evidence: This establishes the research gap that the paper addresses.

claim: Available techniques for measuring NP release include microdialysis.
source: Available techniques for measuring NP release include microdialysis (Kendrick, 1990)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Available techniques for measuring NP release include antibody-coated microprobes.
source: antibody-coated microprobes (Schaible et al., 1990)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GFP-tagged propeptides have been visualized by standard fluorescence microscopy.
source: GFP-tagged propeptides visualized either by standard fluorescence microscopy (van den Pol, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GFP-tagged propeptides have been visualized by TIRF imaging of cultured neurons.
source: or by TIRF imaging of cultured neurons (Xia et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In Drosophila, a fusion between rat Atrial Natriuretic Peptide/Factor (ANP/F) and GFP was used to investigate neuropeptide trafficking at the fly neuromuscular junction.
source: In Drosophila, a fusion between rat Atrial Natriuretic Peptide/Factor (ANP/F) and GFP was used to investigate neuropeptide trafficking at the fly neuromuscular junction (NMJ) (Rao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ANP-GFP release was measured indirectly as a decrease in fluorescence intensity at nerve terminals on a time-scale of seconds.
source: Release was measured indirectly, as a decrease in ANP-GFP fluorescence intensity at nerve terminals reporting residual unreleased peptide, on a time-scale of seconds (Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: None of the existing methods combines NP specificity, genetically addressable cell type-specificity, high temporal resolution and applicability to in vivo preparations.
source: None of these methods combines NP specificity, genetically addressable cell type-specificity, high temporal resolution and applicability to in vivo preparations (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a comparison table in the supplementary materials.

claim: Neuropeptides are synthesized as precursors, sorted into dense core vesicles (DCVs), post-translationally modified and cleaved into active forms prior to release.
source: Neuropeptides are synthesized as precursors, sorted into dense core vesicles (DCVs), post-translationally modified and cleaved into active forms prior to release (Taghert and Veenstra, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: An optimal in vivo real-time NP release reporter should include a reporter domain that reflects the physico-chemical contrast between the intravesicular milieu and the extracellular space.
source: We reasoned that an optimal in vivo real-time NP release reporter should include (1) a reporter domain that reflects the physico-chemical contrast between the intravesicular milieu and the extracellular space (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a design principle stated by the authors and illustrated in a figure.

claim: An optimal in vivo real-time NP release reporter should include a sorting domain that ensures its selective trafficking into DCVs.
source: and (2) a sorting domain that ensures its selective trafficking into DCVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a design principle stated by the authors and illustrated in a figure.

claim: The NP precursor may function as the sorting domain, as suggested by studies of DCV fusion using pIAPP-EGFP and NPY-pHluorin in cultured neurons.
source: The NP precursor may function as the sorting domain, suggested by studies of DCV fusion using pIAPP-EGFP (Barg et al., 2002) and NPY-pHluorin (Zhu et al., 2007) in cultured neurons
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The NP precursor may function as the sorting domain, as suggested by studies using ANP-GFP in Drosophila.
source: or ANP-GFP in Drosophila (Rao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A total of 54 constructs were tested in the screening pipeline.
source: A total of 54 constructs were tested.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach.

claim: Optimal trafficking was achieved by substituting the reporter for the NP precursor C-terminal domain that follows the final peptide.
source: We found that optimal trafficking was achieved by substituting the reporter for the NP precursor C-terminal domain that follows the final peptide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the screening experiments shown in the figure.

claim: The dibasic cleavage site C-terminal to the final peptide was removed to maintain covalent linkage with the reporter domain.
source: In order to maintain covalent linkage with the reporter domain, we removed the dibasic cleavage site C-terminal to the final peptide.
evidence: This is a design decision made by the authors.

claim: The DCV lumen has lower pH (5.5–6.75) compared to the extracellular space (pH 7.3).
source: The DCV lumen has lower pH and free calcium (pH = 5.5–6.75, [Ca2+]~30 µM) compared to the extracellular space (pH = 7.3, [Ca2+]~2 mM) (Mitchell et al., 2001; Sturman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The DCV lumen has lower free calcium (~30 µM) compared to the extracellular space (~2 mM).
source: The DCV lumen has lower pH and free calcium (pH = 5.5–6.75, [Ca2+]~30 µM) compared to the extracellular space (pH = 7.3, [Ca2+]~2 mM) (Mitchell et al., 2001; Sturman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Reporters based on pHluorins did not perform well in the authors' hands.
source: Reporters based on pHluorins (Miesenböck et al., 1998) did not perform well in our hands
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results.

claim: The calcium sensitivity threshold of GCaMP6s is below the calcium concentration in both DCVs and the extracellular space.
source: The calcium sensitivity threshold of GCaMP6s is below the calcium concentration in both DCVs and the extracellular space.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of GCaMP6s.

claim: GCaMP6s fluorescence is quenched in the acidic DCV lumen.
source: However, GCaMP6s fluorescence is quenched in the acidic DCV lumen (Barykina et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GCaMP6s can function as a dual calcium/pH indicator.
source: enabling it to function as a dual calcium/pH indicator (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of GCaMP6s and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The dual calcium/pH sensitivity of GCaMP6s should boost the contrast between fluorescence in unreleased vs. released DCVs.
source: These key properties should boost the contrast between GCaMP6s fluorescence in unreleased vs. released DCVs, potentially allowing us to trace NP release at the cellular level in vivo.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the properties of GCaMP6s.

claim: The Drosophila larval NMJ was used to test NPRRANP for proof-of-principle experiments.
source: Initially for proof-of-principle experiments, we used the Drosophila larval NMJ to test NPRRANP, a GCaMP6s fusion with rat ANP (Burke et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach.

claim: NMJ terminals are large, individually identifiable, and easy to image and record.
source: NMJ terminals are large, individually identifiable, and easy to image and record.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the experimental system.

claim: Type Ib and Type Is boutons contain mostly synaptic vesicles and few DCVs.
source: In particular, boutons on muscle 12/13 are diverse -- Type Ib and Type Is boutons contain mostly synaptic vesicles and few DCVs
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Type III boutons contain an abundance of DCVs but no synaptic vesicles.
source: while Type III boutons contain an abundance of DCVs but no synaptic vesicles (Menon et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Type III-specific GAL4 drivers are available.
source: moreover, Type III-specific GAL4 drivers are available (Koon and Budnik, 2012) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The distribution of NPRRANP overlapped that of Bursicon, an NP endogenously expressed in Type III neurons.
source: Moreover, the distribution of NPRRANP overlapped that of Bursicon (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), an NP that is endogenously expressed in Type III neurons (Loveall and Deitcher, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure and a citation.

claim: Both GCaMP and Bursicon immunoreactivity were strongest within boutons, consistent with the known subcellular localization of DCVs.
source: Both GCaMP and Bursicon immunoreactivity were strongest within boutons, consistent with the known subcellular localization of DCVs (Gorczyca and Budnik, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and a citation.

claim: Glutamate is the only known canonical neurotransmitter used at the larval NMJ.
source: Glutamate is the only known canonical neurotransmitter used at the larval NMJ (Menon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In Type Ib neurons, vGluT staining was observed as patches with a dim center, which may reflect clustered SVs.
source: In Type Ib neurons (which contain relatively few DCVs relative to SVs [Menon et al., 2013]), vGluT staining was observed as patches with a dim center, which may reflect clustered SVs
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemistry with an interpretation.

claim: In Type Ib neurons, NPRRANP immunoreactivity was seen in dispersed, non-overlapping punctae.
source: while NPRRANP immunoreactivity was seen in dispersed, non-overlapping punctae (Figure 1C, α-GFP, inset).
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemistry shown in the figure.

claim: In Type III neurons, NPRRs were strongly expressed but no vGluT immunoreactivity was detected.
source: In Type III neurons, NPRRs were strongly expressed but no vGluT immunoreactivity was detected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemistry shown in the figure.

claim: The subcellular distribution of NPRR in larval NMJ neurons is similar to that of other DCV-targeted markers previously used in this system.
source: The subcellular distribution of this NPRR in larval NMJ neurons, therefore, is similar to that of other DCV-targeted markers previously used in this system (Rao et al., 2001; Shakiryanova et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by citations.

claim: The subcellular distribution of NPRR appears to reflect exclusion from SVs.
source: and appears to reflect exclusion from SVs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Immuno-Electron microscopy was employed to investigate the subcellular localization of NPRRs at the nanometer scale.
source: Therefore, we employed Immuno-Electron microscopy (Immuno-EM) to investigate the subcellular localization of NPRRs at the nanometer scale.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach.

source: To maximize antigenicity for Immuno-EM, we generated constructs that replaced GCaMP6s with GFP (NPRRANP-GFP;).

claim: NPRRANP-GFP showed dense labeling in association with DCVs.
source: NPRRANP-GFP showed dense labeling in association with DCVs (Figure 1D, arrows)

claim: NPRRANP-GFP is localized to DCVs.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that NPRRANP-GFP is localized to DCVs.

claim: NPRRANP-GCaMP6s is similarly packaged in DCVs as NPRRANP-GFP.
source: By extension, they suggest that NPRRANP-GCaMP6s (which has an identical structure to NPRRANP-GFP except for the modifications that confer calcium sensitivity) is similarly packaged in DCVs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity between the two constructs.

claim: NPRRANP-GFP and NPRRANP-GCaMP6s show indistinguishable distributions by immunofluorescence.
source: While these two reporters show indistinguishable distributions by immunofluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence shown in the figure.

claim: The authors cannot formally exclude that the substitution of GCaMP for GFP may subtly alter subcellular localization of the NPRR in a manner undetectable by light microscopy.
source: we cannot formally exclude that the substitution of GCaMP for GFP may subtly alter subcellular localization of the NPRR in a manner undetectable by light microscopy.

claim: 70 Hz electrical stimulation is a frequency reported to trigger NP release as measured by ANF-GFP fluorescence decrease.
source: We delivered 4 trials of 70 Hz electrical stimulation to the nerve bundle, a frequency reported to trigger NP release as measured by ANF-GFP fluorescence decrease (Rao et al., 2001; Shakiryanova et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The stimulation paradigm used an extracellular calcium concentration that promotes full fusion mode.
source: and used an extracellular calcium concentration that promotes full fusion mode (Alés et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The stimulation paradigm produced a relative increase in NPRRANP fluorescence intensity (ΔF/F), whose peak magnitude increased across successive trials.
source: This stimulation paradigm produced a relative increase in NPRRANP fluorescence intensity (ΔF/F), whose peak magnitude increased across successive trials (Figure 2A, red bars and 2D; Video 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1, A1 vs. A7).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the calcium imaging experiments shown in the figures.

claim: NPRRANP responses showed a tri-phasic temporal pattern: rising, falling, and recovering phases.
source: Responses in each trial showed a tri-phasic temporal pattern: (1) In the 'rising' phase, NPRRANP ∆F/F peaked 0.5–5 secs after stimulation onset
evidence: This is a direct observation from the calcium imaging experiments.

claim: NPRRANP ∆F/F peaked 0.5–5 secs after stimulation onset, in contrast to the virtually instantaneous peak seen in positive control specimens expressing conventional GCaMP6s in Type III neurons.
source: in contrast to the virtually instantaneous peak seen in positive control specimens expressing conventional GCaMP6s in Type III neurons (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is a comparison between NPRR and control shown in the figures.

claim: The NPRRANP latency to peak was similar to the reported DCV fusion latency following depolarization in hippocampal neurons.
source: The NPRRANP latency to peak was similar to the reported DCV fusion latency following depolarization in hippocampal neurons (Xia et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by a citation.

claim: The delay in NPRRANP response is thought to reflect the kinetic difference between calcium influx and DCV exocytosis due to the loose association between DCVs and calcium channels.
source: This delay is thought to reflect the kinetic difference between calcium influx and DCV exocytosis due to the loose association between DCVs and calcium channels (Xia et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the falling phase, NPRRANP ∆F/F began to decline 1–5 s before the termination of each stimulation trial, presumably reflecting depletion of the available pool of releasable vesicles.
source: (2) In the 'falling' phase, NPRRANP ∆F/F began to decline 1–5 s before the termination of each stimulation trial, presumably reflecting depletion of the available pool of releasable vesicles.
evidence: This is an observation with an interpretation.

claim: GCaMP6s fluorescence did not return to baseline until after stimulation offset.
source: In contrast, GCaMP6s fluorescence did not return to baseline until after stimulation offset (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is an observation from the control experiments shown in the figures.

claim: NPRRANP exhibited an 'undershoot' (∆F/F below baseline) during the post-stimulation intervals, followed by a 'recovering' phase.
source: (3) Finally, unlike GCaMP6s, NPRRANP exhibited an 'undershoot' (∆F/F below baseline) during the post-stimulation intervals, followed by a 'recovering' phase (Figure 2A; Figures 2C,I1–4).
evidence: This is an observation from the calcium imaging experiments shown in the figures.

claim: The undershoot may reflect dilution of released fluorescent NPRR molecules by diffusion into the synaptic cleft.
source: This undershoot may reflect dilution of released fluorescent NPRR molecules by diffusion into the synaptic cleft (van den Pol, 2012)
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Recovery may reflect DCV replenishment in the boutons from vesicles proximal to the imaged release site.
source: while recovery may reflect DCV replenishment in the boutons from vesicles proximal to the imaged release site.

claim: NPRRANP fluorescence was preferentially accumulated within boutons.
source: Because NPRRANP fluorescence was preferentially accumulated within boutons

claim: The time-averaged ratio of bouton/IBI ΔF/F was significantly higher for NPRRANP than for GCaMP6s, particularly during later stimulation trials.
source: The time-averaged ratio of bouton/IBI ΔF/F (see Materials and Methods) was significantly higher for NPRRANP than for GCaMP6s, particularly during later stimulation trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, green bars, S2-4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the imaging experiments shown in the figure.

claim: NPRRANP signals are preferentially observed in boutons, where DCVs are located, and do not reflect differences in cytoplasmic free Ca2+ levels between these regions as detected by GCaMP6s.
source: This contrast indicates that NPRRANP signals are preferentially observed in boutons, where DCVs are located, and do not reflect differences in cytoplasmic free Ca2+ levels between these regions as detected by GCaMP6s.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison between NPRR and GCaMP6s.

claim: Tetanus toxin light chain (TNT) blocks vesicle fusion at terminals by cleaving n-synaptobrevin.
source: To test definitively if NPRRANP ∆F/F signals are dependent upon NP release, we blocked vesicle fusion at terminals of Type III neurons using expression of tetanus toxin light chain (TNT) (Sweeney et al., 1995), a protease that cleaves n-synaptobrevin, a v-snare required for DCV fusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) (Xu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TNT expression completely abolished stimulation-induced ∆F/F increases from NPRRANP.
source: TNT expression completely abolished stimulation-induced ∆F/F increases from NPRRANP, while TNTimp did not (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the TNT experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Both the ∆F/F peaks and inter-stimulation undershoots were diminished by TNT.
source: Further analysis revealed that both the ∆F/F peaks and inter-stimulation undershoots were diminished by TNT (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the TNT experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Neither TNT nor TNTimp affected the kinetics of GCaMP6s signals in Type III neurons.
source: In contrast, neither TNT nor TNTimp affected the kinetics of GCaMP6s signals in Type III neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), which report cytosolic Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is an observation from the control experiments shown in the figure.

claim: NPRRANP signals specifically reflect DCV release.
source: Taken together, these data support the idea that NPRRANP signals specifically reflect DCV release.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TNT experiments.

claim: ANP is a rat NP that lacks a Drosophila homolog.
source: ANP is a rat NP that lacks a Drosophila homolog (Rao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: NPRRdTK is one of 6 different reporter variants generated from the Drosophila neuropeptide precursor, DTK.
source: To determine whether our method could be applied to detect the release of a specific, endogenous fly NP, we tested NPRRdTK, one of 6 different reporter variants we initially generated from the Drosophila neuropeptide precursor, DTK (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach.

claim: DTK yields multiple NP derivatives.
source: In contrast to ANP which encodes a single peptide, DTK yields multiple NP derivatives (Winther et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: NPRRdTK, like NPRRANP, was localized to DCVs as confirmed by light microscopy and Immuno-EM.
source: Light microscopy (Figure 3A) and Immuno-EM (Figure 3B, arrows) confirmed that NPRRdTK, like NPRRANP, was localized to DCVs (DCV/bouton ~ 22.19, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and EM data shown in the figures.

claim: Using the Type III-specific GAL4 driver to express NPRRdTK and the same stimulation protocol as used for NPRRANP, the basic tri-phasic response profile was also observed.
source: Using the Type III-specific GAL4 driver to express NPRRdTK and the same stimulation protocol as used for NPRRANP, the basic tri-phasic response profile was also observed (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the calcium imaging experiments shown in the figure.

claim: For NPRRdTK, peak heights and baseline fluorescence fell progressively with successive stimulation trials, in contrast to NPRRANP where the first peak and undershoot were lower.
source: However, peak heights and baseline fluorescence fell progressively with successive stimulation trials (Figure 3E), in contrast to NPRRANP where the first peak and undershoot were lower (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is a comparison between NPRRdTK and NPRRANP shown in the figures.

claim: The reason for the difference in response kinetics between NPRRdTK and NPRRANP is currently unclear.
source: The reason for this difference is currently unclear.

source: For both NPRRANP and NPRRdTK (Figure 4A–B), the peak responses showed a positive correlation with stimulation frequency, analogous to that observed using cytosolic GCaMP6s (Figure 4C).

source: In Type III neurons, the responses of both NPRRs to stimulation frequencies < 30 Hz (1,5,10,20 Hz) were not statistically significant from zero.

source: while NPRRdTK showed a higher stimulation threshold and lower sensitivity (30 Hz: 3.57%, 50 Hz: 24.67% Normalized peak ∆F/F).

claim: In Type Ib neurons, significant increases in ∆F/F could be observed at frequencies as low as 10 Hz.

claim: The reason for the difference in NPRR threshold between Type III and Type Ib neurons is unknown, but parallels their difference in GCaMP6s response to electrical stimulation.
source: The reason for the difference in NPRR threshold between Type III and Type Ib neurons is unknown, but parallels their difference in GCaMP6s response to electrical stimulation (Figure 4C vs. Figure 4F).

source: Notably, although NPRRANP and NPRRdTK presented distinct response profiles in Type III neurons, their performance in Type Ib neurons was more similar (Figure 4A vs. Figure 4B; cf. Figure 4D vs. Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a comparison of results shown in the figures.

source: In summary, the differences in performance we observed between the two NPRRs appeared to be specific to Type III neurons, and were minor in comparison to the differences in performance of both reporters between the two cell classes.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparative results.

claim: The reason for the differences between NPRRANP and NPRRdTK sensitivity and kinetics in Type III neurons is unknown but may reflect differences in how well these reporters compete with the high levels of endogenous neuropeptide (Bursicon) for packaging, transport or release.
source: The reason for the differences between NPRRANP and NPRRdTK sensitivity and kinetics in Type III neurons is unknown but may reflect differences in how well these reporters compete with the high levels of endogenous neuropeptide (Bursicon) for packaging, transport or release.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed differences.

claim: The method presented provides proof-of-principle for detecting the release of different neuropeptides in intact neural tissue, with subcellular spatial and sub-second temporal resolution.
source: Here we present proof-of-principle for a method to detect the release of different neuropeptides in intact neural tissue, with subcellular spatial and sub-second temporal resolution.

source: NPRR responses exhibited triphasic kinetics, including rising, falling and recovering phases.

claim: TNT has been shown to effectively block NP release in many systems.
source: To test if NPRRANP ∆F/F signals are dependent on NP release, we expressed the light chain of tetanus toxin (TNT), a reagent shown to effectively block NP release in many (McNabb and Truman, 2008; Hentze et al., 2015; Zandawala et al., 2018), if not all (Umezaki et al., 2011), systems.
